turns.user: Compare the free tiers of Vercel, Netlify and Cloudflare Pages for a small side project.
turns.answer:
For a small side project, Cloudflare Pages has the most generous free tier on paper, Netlify has the clearest hard caps, and Vercel's Hobby plan is limited to non-commercial use.

| | Vercel Hobby | Netlify Free | Cloudflare Pages Free |
|---|---|---|---|
| Price | $0/mo. The perfect starting place for your web app or personal project. | $0 forever | Free (Workers Free plan) |
| Bandwidth / requests | 100GB bandwidth, 1M CDN Requests, 4 hours Active CPU, 1M function invocations. | Monthly credits: 300 (bandwidth is drawn from these) | Pages has no bandwidth cap in the docs I found; Workers Free has a daily request limit of 100,000 requests |
| Builds | Deployments Created per Day: 100 | 1 concurrent build | You can deploy up to 500 times per month on the Free plan. |
| Files / size | Static File uploads: 100 MB | Credits-based | Cloudflare Pages sites can contain up to 20,000 files on the Free plan. |
| Commercial use | Non-commercial only. | Allowed | Not restricted in the pages I found |
| Over the limit | you are limited to the usage caps and cannot purchase additional usage. | When credits run out, projects pause until the next billing cycle. | Not verified |

Recommendation: if the project is commercial, Cloudflare Pages or Netlify; Vercel's free tier only works for non-commercial use. Figures are from vendor pages as of this search, and the Cloudflare build cap comes from a community answer, so confirm it in their docs before committing.

setup.user: Which managed Postgres hosting is cheapest for a small app: Neon, Supabase, or AWS RDS?
setup.answer:
The cheapest option for a small app that isn't always busy is Neon. Its paid plan has no monthly minimum and bills only for active compute, and its free tier covers small projects. Neon's Free plan is $0/month and includes 100 projects, with 100 CU-hours of compute per project and 1 GB of storage. Idle compute is not billed: when there's no traffic, the compute suspends and you stop accruing CU-hours; storage continues to bill at $0.35/GB-month on paid plans.

Supabase is the more expensive of the two managed options for a small app. Pro is $25/month and includes the first project. Paid plans include $10 in Compute Credits, which cover one project running on the Micro/Nano Compute size or portions of other Compute sizes. Supabase Free does not pause projects on Pro, though its free tier pauses after inactivity.

AWS RDS has no minimum, but it bills by instance-hour and requires you to provision the instance. Amazon RDS is free to try and you pay only for what you use with no minimum fees. The Free plan is available on db.t3.micro and db.t4g.micro instances for the following 4 engines, but that is limited to new accounts, and the RDS instance has no scale-to-zero, so a small always-on instance is typically the lowest-cost choice after that.

Bottom line: Neon is the cheapest for a small or intermittent app. Prices are as of 3 Nov 2026 per Neon's pricing page and Supabase's pricing page; I did not get a current RDS per-instance price.
